## From the repo

### Intent
What this repository is for, from its .zbuild/vision.md. It steers every
choice you make.


### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

### Guidance for this stage
This repository's guidance for this stage (.zbuild/prompts/design-overrides.md).
It adds to your job; it cannot take any part of it away.

### zBuild design-stage overrides

This repository's own additions to design's job (ADR-032/033): the sets in this
repository that break by OMISSION, and how a design accounts for them.

#### Rule ABS — a closed set breaks by omission

Some closed sets in this repo break by OMISSION rather than by a stale token you
can grep: the breakage is a MISSING (or orphaned) line, not a changed one. When a
change grows, shrinks, or renames such a set, every enumeration of that set is
wrong by omission — yet there is nothing to grep for, because the defect is the
absent entry. The pipeline's stages are not such a set: which stages run is
template data, not a list the code enumerates.

When a change grows, shrinks or renames a closed set, the design accounts for
every place that enumerates or COUNTS it:

- code or config that enumerates it: a step, naming that code;
- an existing test that enumerates or counts it: a line in the ```supersedes
  block (the test file, the assertion's tag, and why it is now wrong), so the
  test author brings it up to the new set.

Rediscover the places each time; a hardcoded list of them goes stale.

#### How to find them

Enumeration/count sites are most often mock-plugin roster blocks (one call per
member) or literal counts of the set. Rediscover them with:

```
grep -rln '_make_plugin\|_make_role_plugin\|_make_verdict_plugin\|mock_plugin_factory' tests/
grep -rln 'stage\.complete\|plugin\.run\.start\|started .*UTC\|finished .*UTC' tests/
```

Re-run the greps each time — new enumeration sites arrive with new tests, and
the defect (a missing line) leaves no token to search for.

#### Rule ABS-W — a new plugin directory needs a wiki page

A change that creates `plugins/<kind>/<id>/manifest.yaml` also creates
`docs/wiki/plugins/<id>.md`, with a prose opening paragraph: a step names it,
and a `[doc]` SPEC says what it must tell a reader. The `lint-doc-freshness`
gate (`scripts/lib/lint-doc-freshness.sh`) fails the suite when the page is
absent or has no opening paragraph — there is no old value to grep for, because
the defect is the missing new file.

**Exception — `kind: persona` plugins:** persona manifests are data-only (no
`plugin.sh`, no hooks) and share one page, `docs/wiki/plugins/personas.md`. A new
persona adds its id there instead of a page of its own; `lint-doc-freshness`
checks that every persona id appears in that page, and a per-id persona page is
an orphan it fails.

## What you own

Your job: write the design — the change's decisions and its acceptance contract — in the working copy at the path below. When it passes design's checks it becomes design.md. Save it as you go: a design on disk when your time runs out still counts.

Choose the smallest design that does what the requirements need, and follow the
patterns the code already follows rather than adding a one-off.

The working copy already holds YOUR LATEST DESIGN (below). Change only what needs to change.

Previous work may hold findings from later stages. A finding is yours only if changing the design would fix it: its acceptance contract. Answer each of those in the design. Leave the others — a bug in the code, a test that does not run, a lint failure — and do not investigate them. In a Findings section of the design, list every finding: what you changed for it, or why you left it. You do not debug code or work out why a test fails.

Write the design document to this EXACT absolute path:
  /home/runner/work/_temp/zbuild-state/artifacts/design-draft.md

The design document MUST include:
1. A brief architectural decision summary (goal, context, decision).
2. A ```steps block: the ordered work items that change the code, one per
   line, each with the areas of the code it is about:
```steps
- <what to do, in one sentence> | areas: path/to/file1, path/to/file2
```
   The build follows them in order. A step is code work only: it names no file
   or folder in the test folders. What you own of the tests is your SPECs:
   they say what the tests must prove. The test author writes the tests —
   which cases, in which files and how.

3. A ```acceptance block listing what this change must deliver. Each line is
   one requirement: an id, a status, and ONE behaviour someone could observe and test.
   The id describes the SPEC: DS, then 3 or 4 capital letters or digits,
   starting with a letter, that say what it is about, a dash, and a number —
   DSLOOP-1 for a SPEC about loop state. The id is also the tag its test
   carries, [DSLOOP-1]:
   - The highest number each code has had, removed ones counted, and in the repository's tests: DSADR 8, DSBUD 1, DSCLA 22, DSCLM 9, DSDEL 1, DSEND 1, DSFRSH 1, DSFSTG 9, DSLOOP 1, DSPRB 6, DSWORK 9. A new SPEC with one of these codes takes the next number; a new code starts at 1.
   - A SPEC you keep keeps its id.
   - REMOVED: only for a SPEC in the last design that passed — one you drop
     gets a line `REMOVED: <id> — <why>`, kept in every later design. An id
     that only a rejected try wrote is not taken: write no REMOVED line for it.
   - Never use one of the issue's requirement ids as a SPEC id.
   A design written with old ids (SPEC-1, or ids not starting with DS) gives
   each SPEC a new id once; the old ids need no REMOVED line.
   A requirement that asks for several things gets one SPEC per thing, each
   naming the same requirement id in covers: — never one SPEC that joins them with "and" or ";".
   Each SPEC is checked against one assertion, so a SPEC that promises two
   things is never fully met by it.

   Under its line, each [code] and [done] SPEC says its behaviour in parts, one
   per line, indented ([no-code] may too):
   - `Given:` the situation the code is in before the When — never the steps a test takes to get there. Optional; any number.
   - `When:` the one action — exactly one When per SPEC: a second action is a second SPEC.
   - `Then:` something a test can observe after the When — an output, a
     result, a file the code writes, an event. One or more. Never what a file
     or a test contains, and never how a test looks for it.
   - `And:` adds another line to the Given or Then above it.
   How a test sets this up, checks it and cleans up after it is the test's, not
   the requirement's.

   The status says what work the requirement needs. Look at the code before you choose:
   - `DSLOOP-1[code]:` — it needs code. Its test must fail on the code as it is before your change, and pass after it.
     If the code already does it, it is not [code]: its test would already pass, and the build stalls on it.
     Every requirement except a [doc] one describes what someone could see happen, not what a file contains: not "x.sh contains foo", "file y exists" or "the test file has both cases" — no test can prove those.
   - `DSLOOP-2[no-code]:` — it needs work that changes no behaviour: a test,
     config, or a refactor. Its test must pass after the change; it need not fail before.
   - `DSDOCS-1[doc]:` — it changes a doc. It has no test and no Given/When/Then: say, on its one line, what the doc must tell a reader
     (the guide says a resume puts back what every finished stage wrote). The doc is read to check it.
   - `DSGARD-1[done]:` — the code from before your change already does it. Name the evidence at the end of the line, after ` evidence: ` —
     a file by its path from the repository root, then ` | `, then one line of it copied as it is
     (scripts/x.sh | run_guard()), or an existing test file named alone.
     The text must be in the file on the commit this branch started from: code this work added is not
     done yet, so it is [code]. A [done] SPEC still gets a test: it must pass after the change, and it
     need not fail before — it proves the finished change still does what the old code did.
   Every requirement carries one of the four. A change that edits code needs at least one [code] requirement.

   You name no test file, and no list of the files the change touches. The
   tests are written after the design, by the test author, wherever they
   belong, and a requirement's test is found by its tag. Each [code] assertion is also run against the code from before your
   change and must fail there, so write ONE requirement per assertion — then
   each behaviour is checked on its own.

The ```acceptance block format:
```acceptance
DSLOOP-1[code]: <one new behaviour this change introduces>
  Given: <the situation the code is in>
  When: <the one action>
  Then: <what a test can observe after it>
  And: <another thing a test can observe>
DSLOOP-2[no-code]: <a test, config or a refactor that changes no behaviour>
DSDOCS-1[doc]: <what a doc must tell a reader>
DSGARD-1[done]: <something the code already does> evidence: scripts/x.sh | run_guard()
  When: <the action>
  Then: <what the code from before this change already does>
REMOVED: DSLOOP-3 — <why this SPEC was dropped>
WIRING: <the existing file that calls the new code>
```

WIRING: Which existing file calls the new code?
- Name the existing file whose code calls (or loads) the new behaviour:
  the place a running program reaches it from. It is not the file that
  implements the behaviour, and it is not a test. If that file were put back
  to how it is today, at least one test of this change would fail.
- A list, schema or config entry is never this file: adding a name to an event
  list, a schema or a config list changes no behaviour on its own.
- One path per line; several lines are allowed:
    WIRING:
    plugins/agent/build/plugin.sh
    core/pipeline/runner.sh
- If nothing calls the new code yet (a helper used later), write
  `WIRING: none`.
- After the build, the file you name is put back to its old version (everything
  else kept), and at least one test must then fail. That is how the pipeline
  checks you named the right file.

Existing checks this change makes wrong: when the change alters a
behaviour an EXISTING assertion pins (one that is not a SPEC of this contract),
list it in a ```supersedes block — one line per check, the testfile path,
the assertion's tag, and why it is now wrong:
```supersedes
tests/unit/foo-test.sh [SPEC-3]: `verdict` is now the v2 result's status key, not a merge decision
```
Updating those checks to the new behaviour is part of writing the tests. Omit
the block when no existing check changes meaning.

Before you add a file or a mechanism, find what already owns the job: the
plugin kinds in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, the ADRs for the area, the existing plugins
and libraries. Build on it, not beside it. Name in the design what you found and
why you used it or not.

A requirement you do not understand — the issue could mean either of two
things — is not guessed in silence. Write one line for it in the design,
outside the fenced blocks:
UNCLEAR: <id> | <the question> | <what you assumed>
where <id> is the requirement's id. Then carry on with that assumption: design
the change as if it were the answer. The question and your assumption are
shown to the people who can answer it.

Keep the prose focused and under 200 lines (the acceptance block may be as
long as completeness requires).


## What you judge against

The issue may describe a solution as well as the
problem. A section that records a decision (for example "Decision:") is binding: follow it.
Anything else it proposes — an approach, a file list, a claim that
some files or tests are unaffected — is a starting point, not the answer: check
it against the code yourself and come up with your own design. Where yours
differs, say why.

### Tools
- You MAY use the Read tool to inspect any file in the repository.
- You MAY use the Grep tool to search the whole repository for symbols,
  constants, references, and hardcoded values.
- You MAY use the Glob tool to discover files by pattern.

### The code from before this change
The commit this branch started from is a copy at /home/runner/work/_temp/zbuild-state/base-code. A [done] SPEC is checked
there: to see whether the code from before your change already does something,
open the file there, not in the working copy — the working copy holds every
change this branch made, in this round and in earlier ones.

### Requirements from the issue (each with its id)
- RQCLA-1: When the issue has no `zbuild:claimed` label, the run adds it before the first stage dispatches
- RQCLA-2: When the label is added, the run's run-status comment names the holder: run id and machine, or CI run URL
- RQCLA-3: When the `zbuild:claimed` label is present, the run refuses to start with non-zero exit and no stage dispatched
- RQCLA-4: When refusing to start, the run's message names the holder from the holder's run-status comment
- RQCLA-5: On normal end, the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-6: On failure, the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-7: On interrupt (TERM), the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-8: A run with no issue (goal only) makes no claim and calls no coordinator hook
- RQCLA-9: When the `zbuild:claimed` label is present, the run emits the `pipeline.refused.claimed` event
- RQCLA-10: The `pipeline.refused.claimed` event is registered in `config/event-schema.json`
- RQLAB-1: A local run and a CI run use the same label, `zbuild:claimed`
- RQLAB-2: There is no machine name in the label
- RQADR-1: Amend ADR-005 with: the engine calls the coordinator: `claim` after the admission lock and before the first stage, `release` in the EXIT path
- RQADR-2: Amend ADR-005 with: the single shared label, and that the holder is in the run-status comment
- RQADR-3: Amend ADR-005 to correct the stale parts: selection is not from `config/zbuild.yaml`, and "the engine has no built-in mechanism" no longer holds once the engine calls the coordinator
- RQADR-4: The ADR-005 amendments must include an `## Enforced by` section naming the tests that enforce each statement
- RQADR-5: Amend ADR-059 §4 to note that cross-machine exclusion is the claim coordinator's job, and the admission lock stays for one machine
- RQDOC-1: README.md in plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/ does not reference `claimed:<machine>` labels and reflects the single shared label
- RQCLA-11: Release must survive a second TERM
- RQCLA-12: The coordinator's claim hook adds the `zbuild:claimed` label
- RQCLA-13: The coordinator's release hook removes the `zbuild:claimed` label
- RQARC-1: The label calls (`gh issue edit`) are in `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`
- RQARC-2: Nothing under `core/` calls `gh` for the label
- RQARC-3: The engine claims and releases only through the claim coordinator's `claim` and `release` hooks, called through the plugin registry
- RQCLA-14: A test that registers a stub claim coordinator sees its `claim` hook called before the first stage and its `release` hook called on exit.

Every requirement above must be covered by at least one SPEC. End each SPEC line with ` covers: ` and the ids of the requirements it covers, before any ` evidence: ` — for example `DSLOOP-1[code]: <behaviour> covers: <requirement ids>`. A requirement the code already meets is covered by a [done] SPEC with evidence.

### Terms from the issue — each means this, and only this
Each term below means this, and only this, everywhere in this issue.

- **Run-status comment:** the comment ADR-064 already posts and edits for every run (`scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`). Not a new comment.
- **Holder:** who has the claim. Locally: the run id and the machine's name. In CI: the CI run's URL.
- **Claim coordinator:** the ADR-005 plugin kind; here `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`. The engine calls its `claim` and `release` hooks through the plugin registry. The label calls (`gh issue edit`) live in the plugin, not in `core/`.

Use each term as the issue defines it here, in every SPEC and step.

### Limits from the issue — what this change must not do
- RQMECH-1: Do not build a check of a CI job's status through the GitHub Actions API
- RQMECH-2: Do not build a "do I still hold the claim" check before each stage

Write no SPEC for a limit, and no step that does what one forbids: a limit is met by not building it, and it is checked against the change once it is made.

### YOUR LATEST DESIGN (refine it; Previous work says what moved since you wrote it)
Every claim it makes about the repository — an ADR it relies on, a file it lists, a hook, field or convention it declares — is re-checked against the tree as it is NOW, and every SPEC it keeps against the issue's requirements as they are NOW, not only the new ones: anything that no longer holds is dropped or re-derived — a SPEC a requirement now contradicts is rewritten or removed — and the design says what changed and why. Keep what still holds; do not start over.

# Design — GitHub label claim (#1764)

## Goal

Prevent two concurrent zBuild runs on the same issue from overlapping across machines using a
GitHub label (`zbuild:claimed`) as a soft cross-machine claim. The existing local flock
(`core/state/issue-lock.sh`) remains for intra-machine serialisation; this change adds the
inter-machine layer on top of it.

## Context

`core/state/issue-lock.sh` is a filesystem flock: effective on one host, invisible from another.
Issue #1764 asks for a GitHub label that any run can see before it starts. The run-status sidecar
already posts a progress comment on the issue (ADR-064, `scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`);
the holder string goes into that comment, satisfying RQADR-2 without a separate claim comment.

The base code's `claim_coordinator_claim` uses `claimed:<machine>` as the label. This change
replaces that with the single shared label `zbuild:claimed`. RQARC-3 and RQCLA-14 require the
engine to call the coordinator's hooks through the plugin registry (via `plugin_hook_call`), so
that a test can substitute a stub coordinator through the discovery mechanism.

## Decision

**`plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh`**: replace `claimed:<machine>` with the
shared label `zbuild:claimed` in both `claim_coordinator_claim` and `claim_coordinator_release`;
add `_ccgl_read_holder` to read the holder from the issue's run-status comment; on conflict,
`claim_coordinator_claim` returns `{"acquired": false, "holder": "<extracted_holder>"}`;
remove any `source` of `core/claim/claim.sh` from `plugin.sh` — the dependency arrow is
one-way (`claim.sh` → (registry) → `plugin.sh`).

**`scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh`**: add `<!-- zbuild-holder: ... -->` in `rsc_render_header`
immediately after the run-id marker: CI path uses `<!-- zbuild-holder: <CI_URL> -->`; local
path uses `<!-- zbuild-holder: run_id=<id> machine=<host> -->`.

**`core/claim/claim.sh`** (new wiring bridge via plugin registry): sources
`core/plugin-registry/registry.sh` via `$_ZBUILD_ROOT` at top (idempotent — `runner.sh`
sources `claim.sh` at line 33, before `registry.sh` at line 46, so `claim.sh` must load it);
`zbuild_claim_build_holder` builds and exports `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER` using `${HOSTNAME}` bash
variable (no fork); `zbuild_claim_acquire <issue>`: skip if issue is empty — returns 0
immediately without calling `discover_plugins` or any coordinator hook; calls
`discover_plugins "${ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT:-$_ZBUILD_ROOT/plugins}"` and filters for the first
plugin with `kind: claim-coordinator` to obtain `coordinator_dir`, stored in
`_ZBUILD_COORDINATOR_DIR`; calls `plugin_hook_call "$coordinator_dir" claim "$issue"` with
stdout captured; parses the JSON for `acquired`/`holder`; on `acquired: false` sanitizes the
holder string (strip ANSI escape codes via `sed`) and stores in `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER`, returns
1; on backend error (no coordinator found, or non-zero hook exit) returns 0 with a stderr
warning (graceful degradation — the intra-machine flock still serialises); on success sets
`_ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED`; `zbuild_claim_release <issue>`: skip if `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED` is
unset — returns 0 immediately without calling any coordinator hook; MUST call
`unset _ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED` BEFORE calling
`plugin_hook_call "$_ZBUILD_COORDINATOR_DIR" release "$issue"` (makes second call a no-op —
this is the idempotency RQCLA-11 relies on); no direct `gh` calls anywhere in
`core/claim/claim.sh`.

For non-`run` hooks `plugin_hook_call` goes straight to `_plugin_hook_call_once` (no retry
loop, no output scan). The hook runs in a background subshell that is immediately waited on;
its JSON stdout flows through to `plugin_hook_call`'s stdout and is captured by the outer
`$( )`.

**`core/pipeline/runner.sh`**: source `core/claim/claim.sh` at top (already in place); call
`zbuild_claim_build_holder` before sidecar spawn; call `zbuild_claim_acquire` after
`zbuild_issue_lock_acquire`; on refusal emit `pipeline.refused.claimed`, print holder via
`printf '%s\n'` (not `error()` which uses `echo -e` and would interpret backslash sequences in
an attacker-controlled holder string), return 1; call `zbuild_claim_release` in
`_runner_abort_trap` after the `trap '' INT TERM` guard, with a `declare -F` guard; add
`zbuild_claim_release || true` to both early-failure return paths that currently have only
`zbuild_run_cap_release || true`.

**`config/event-schema.json`**: register `pipeline.refused.claimed` following the pattern of
`pipeline.refused.issue_locked`.

**ADR-005**: amend for RQADR-1 through RQADR-4; extend the `## Enforced by` section.

**ADR-059 §4**: note that cross-machine exclusion is the coordinator's job; add `[DSCLA-3]` to
the `## Enforced by` entry for the §4 cross-machine statement.

The label `zbuild:claimed` contains no hostname (RQLAB-2). Check-then-label is not atomic at
GitHub; two racing machines may both succeed. Known limitation; strict mutex is out of scope
(RQMECH-1, RQMECH-2).

UNCLEAR: RQADR-2 | "the holder is in the run-status comment" — which comment is this? | Assumed:
the ADR-064 run-status comment (`scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`), not a new one.

```steps
- Amend plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh: replace `claimed:<machine>` with `zbuild:claimed` in claim_coordinator_claim (remove local our_label and machine logic) and in claim_coordinator_release; add _ccgl_read_holder to extract the holder from the issue's run-status comment; claim_coordinator_claim returns {"acquired": false, "holder": "<holder>"} on conflict; remove any source of core/claim/claim.sh from plugin.sh (the dependency arrow is claim.sh→registry→plugin.sh, not the reverse) | areas: plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh
- Update plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/README.md: remove all references to claimed:<machine>; describe the single shared label zbuild:claimed; update ZBUILD_CLAIM_MACHINE_ID row to note it now affects only the holder string in the run-status comment, not the label name | areas: plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/README.md
- Edit scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh: add <!-- zbuild-holder: CI_URL --> (CI) or <!-- zbuild-holder: run_id=X machine=H --> (local) in rsc_render_header after the run_id marker | areas: scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh

## Architecture summary

Dependency arrow: runner.sh → claim.sh → registry.sh; claim.sh → plugin_hook_call → [subshell: plugin.sh]
- plugin.sh MUST NOT source claim.sh (no circular dependency)
- claim.sh DOES NOT source plugin.sh directly
- claim.sh sources registry.sh (idempotent)
- claim.sh uses discover_plugins to find coordinator by kind at call time
- claim.sh calls plugin_hook_call for claim/release hooks
- core/ never calls gh directly for labels (RQARC-2)
- gh calls happen only inside plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh (RQARC-1)
- When issue is empty: zbuild_claim_acquire returns 0 immediately, no discover_plugins, no hook
- When _ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED unset: zbuild_claim_release returns 0 immediately, no hook

## Load order

runner.sh: sources claim.sh before registry.sh
claim.sh sources registry.sh at its own top (idempotent guard prevents double-load)
Registry is available when claim.sh's functions are defined and when they are called.
